So I just wanted to run make sure we were on the, just on track for this move.' No time-box framing or dependability promise offered.
evidence_quotes.their_agenda: Never asked. Rep references a prior move and assumes same scope: 'I know we just kinda did a move for you...It's basically the same thing just reversed.' No open question about concerns or what answers Megan wants.
evidence_quotes.two_layers_deep: N/A — no concerns raised by customer in this call.

evidence_quotes.explicit_ask: Never asked. Rep moves directly to scheduling: 'Did you want to get that scheduled?' and then confirms the date without ever asking 'Would you like our help with your move?' The booking happens by default procedural question, not a clear ask for the business.
evidence_quotes.rate_lock_mentioned: Yes — mentioned in passing: 'Yeah, so there's no deposit to book there's no rescheduling or, or cancellation fee.'

Phone number and crew size (two-man) are not explicitly re-confirmed in the booking close. No notes left about customer's concerns (there were none raised, but this is still a miss in the standard closing routine).

top_strength: Calvin handled the logistical complexity of the uncertain Monday/Tuesday situation smoothly, proactively reassured Megan that there's no rescheduling fee, and coordinated elevator reservations without adding friction.
coaching_note: This was a repeat-customer follow-up call, not a full sales call—skip Section 1's quid pro quo, jump straight to scheduling, and skip the Two Promises entirely because pricing is already established. The rep needs to recognize that pattern and adjust the rubric application, or if this is meant to follow the full script anyway, Calvin must open with a time-boxed framing, never skip the explicit ask for the business, and always deliver the Two Promises even on repeats.
